turns.en: Sam Altman and Greg Brockman founded OpenAI 11 years ago next month, as it happened. Sam is the chief executive. Greg is the president. Almost four years ago, on November 22nd, 2022, they released ChatGPT, built on a model called GPT-3.5, and changed the world. And we've been talking about it basically ever since. More than a billion people—I think it's a little over 1.2 billion now—are using ChatGPT every single week. And we've got about a million questions about the future and everything that's going on around us, as well as issues about security and safety and the economics of the new frontier, the politics of all of this. So please welcome Sam and Greg together. It's great to see you both.
turns.zh: Sam Altman 和 Greg Brockman 在 11 年前的下个月创立了 OpenAI，事情就是这样。Sam 是首席执行官，Greg 是总裁。大约四年前，2022 年 11 月 22 日，他们发布了基于 GPT-3.5 模型的 ChatGPT，改变了世界。从那以后我们基本上一直在谈论它。超过 10 亿人——我想现在略高于 12 亿——每周都在使用 ChatGPT。我们有大约一百万个关于未来的问题，以及围绕我们周围发生的一切，还有关于安全和保障、新前沿的经济学、所有这些的政治问题。所以请欢迎 Sam 和 Greg 一起上台。很高兴见到你们两位。

turns.en: Thank you.
turns.zh: 谢谢。

turns.en: Thanks for having us.
turns.zh: 谢谢邀请我们。

turns.en: There's about a million things to talk about. We have Anthropic's IPO happening tomorrow. We have the Jensen news. You have a new model that just came out yesterday. There are now security concerns—JD Vance is saying back in Washington—and I think in part because of some of these things. And I want to get to all of that. I know you've been asked about the Jensen situation and we were just talking about it backstage, but what do you think? I mean, you've watched this play out. Do you have a—I mean, what I'm curious—have you talked to him about this?
turns.zh: 有大约一百万件事要谈。明天 Anthropic 的 IPO 就要发生了。我们有 Jensen 的新闻。你们昨天刚发布了一个新模型。现在有安全担忧——JD Vance 在华盛顿说——我认为部分是因为其中一些事情。我想谈到所有这些。我知道你们被问过 Jensen 的情况，我们刚刚在后台也谈过，但你们怎么想？我是说，你们看着这件事发展。你们有没有——我很好奇——你们和他谈过这件事吗？

turns.en: Do you want to go first?
turns.zh: 你想先来吗？

turns.en: Either of you?
turns.zh: 你们俩谁先都行？

turns.en: Look, I would say Jensen is singular. No question. And I have talked to him a little bit. My wife and I are friends with him and his family, and so we just reached out personally just to be there for him and his family at this time.
turns.zh: 看，我会说 Jensen 是独一无二的。毫无疑问。我跟他谈过一点。我妻子和他以及他的家人是朋友，所以我们只是私下联系了一下，在这个时刻陪伴他和他的家人。

turns.en: And how's he doing?
turns.zh: 他怎么样？

turns.en: Well, it was a personal private conversation is what I'd say. I think it's obviously a tough time for everyone, but again, I think Nvidia is such an incredible company. I think that what has been built there, what Jensen has built there, it clearly is built to last. And so we're excited to keep partnering and looking to the future.
turns.zh: 嗯，我会说那是一次私人的私下谈话。我认为这显然对每个人来说都是艰难的时刻，但再次，我认为 Nvidia 是一家如此了不起的公司。我认为那里建立的东西，Jensen 在那里建立的东西，显然是为了长久。所以我们很兴奋继续合作并展望未来。

turns.en: Sam, you speak to him, too?
turns.zh: Sam，你也和他谈过吗？

turns.en: I did.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: And?
turns.zh: 然后呢？

turns.en: Jensen took one of the earliest big bets on us. We took a big bet on Nvidia. It's hard to imagine the AI industry without Jensen. I think singular is a great way to describe it.
turns.zh: Jensen 最早对我们下了大赌注之一。我们也对 Nvidia 下了大赌注。很难想象没有 Jensen 的 AI 行业。我认为“独一无二”是一个很好的描述方式。

turns.en: Do you think he—do you think he thinks he can come back when you talk to him?
turns.zh: 你觉得他——当你和他谈话时，你觉得他认为自己能回来吗？

turns.en: Greg and I have a little more empathy towards the situation than the average person. And I will say one thing I did not appreciate was everybody on earth speculating with some random theory here or there. So I will say I wish Jensen the best. I wish Nvidia the best. I don't think the world needs another set of random opinions on what's going to happen here.
turns.zh: Greg 和我对这种情况比普通人更有同理心。我要说一件我不欣赏的事是地球上每个人都在用一些随机的理论在这里或那里猜测。所以我要说，我祝 Jensen 一切顺利。我祝 Nvidia 一切顺利。我不认为世界需要另一组关于这里会发生什么的随机意见。

turns.en: Okay. But let me ask you a philosophical question unrelated to Jensen but related in a way because I think about it a lot. I think about it in the context of this event actually. The idea of the cult of the CEO—so many of the people that are on this stage including both of you. There is a cult of the CEO around them. The idea that some of these companies are so singular and these individuals are so singular and that they can't be run without them. You were pushed out and then came back in part because there was a view that certain people thought that you were both pushed out and came back. I don't like—I don't—again all these differences between the situations tempting to put too much there but I think a large part of what made OpenAI has made OpenAI succeed is that Greg and I have a unique partnership and brought something important to OpenAI and did that over a period of now almost 11 years. Now could the company succeed without us? Yes. But do we together bring something that I think is important to what has driven OpenAI to where it is now? Absolutely. And I think that has been—you know, our partnership together has been one of the most enjoyable parts of this for me over the last 11 years. I remember Greg early on in OpenAI would send me these screenshots and I think he even posted a few on Twitter of like how many hours a week he coded and it was this sort of like legend inside of OpenAI. Now Greg is operating in a different way and you know managing the company with that same ferocity and that is a special thing and I don't want to think about what OpenAI would be like without that. So, is it true that I think people overproject onto any single person their importance to the company? Yes, probably. Do I also think there are people, and I'm very grateful to have gotten to work with Greg for so long as one of these people that do bring something that is very special and very hard to find also? Yes.
turns.zh: 好。但让我问你一个哲学问题，与 Jensen 无关，但某种程度上相关，因为我经常思考它。实际上我是在这个事件的背景下思考它。CEO 崇拜的想法——这个舞台上的很多人包括你们两位。他们周围有 CEO 崇拜。认为其中一些公司如此独特，这些个人如此独特，没有他们公司就无法运营。你被赶出去然后又回来了，部分是因为有一种观点认为某些人认为你们俩都被赶出去又回来了。我不喜欢——我不——再次，所有这些情况之间的差异，很容易在那里放太多东西，但我认为让 OpenAI 成功的一大部分是 Greg 和我有一种独特的合作关系，给 OpenAI 带来了一些重要的东西，并且这样做了将近 11 年。现在公司没有我们能成功吗？是的。但我们一起带来了一些我认为对推动 OpenAI 走到今天很重要的东西吗？绝对。我认为那一直是——你知道，我们的合作关系对我来说是过去 11 年中最愉快的部分之一。我记得早期在 OpenAI，Greg 会给我发这些截图，我想他甚至在 Twitter 上发了几张，比如他每周编码多少小时，这在 OpenAI 内部是一种传奇。现在 Greg 以不同的方式运作，你知道以同样的凶猛管理公司，那是一件特别的事情，我不想想没有那的 OpenAI 会是什么样。所以，人们是否过度投射到任何单个人对公司的的重要性？是的，可能。我是否也认为有些人，我非常感激能和 Greg 一起工作这么久，作为这些人之一，确实带来了一些非常特别且非常难找到的东西？是的。

turns.en: Can you just explain because I don't think we've actually seen both of you together on a stage like this before. You have historically been the face of this company and increasingly Greg you were sort of in the shadow I think but now increasingly are running the business. How do you guys work together? What is this—what is this partnership like and longer term? Do you want to get into the shadow and him to take the stage or how does this—how's this going to work?
turns.zh: 你能解释一下吗，因为我认为我们实际上以前没有在这样的舞台上看到你们俩一起。历史上你一直是这家公司的门面，而 Greg 你越来越——我想你有点在阴影中，但现在越来越多地经营业务。你们怎么合作？这是什么——这种合作关系是什么样的，长期来看？你想进入阴影而让他上台，还是这——这将如何运作？

turns.en: Do you want to go first and I'll take a second?
turns.zh: 你想先来，我接着说？

turns.en: Sure.
turns.zh: 当然。

turns.en: I mean to understand how we work I guess I would rewind to the very beginning of OpenAI. We did this dinner that Sam had put together in July 2015 where we were talking about the idea that became OpenAI. Like was it too late to start a lab with a bunch of the best people to really try to make a positive impact on AGI? And no one could come up with a reason it was sufficiently impossible. So Sam and I driving back to the city together, we looked at each other, we're like, we have to do this. And I was between jobs at the time. So next day I was full-time on it. Sam had a day job, but we were constantly on the phone with each other. Probably like five, six times a day. We would call each other for two minutes at a time, right? Just incredibly rapid fire, just like the highest bandwidth interactions I've had in a professional setting with anyone. Like 100% how how we started, how we operate today. And so probably over the past week, we've probably been on I can't even count dozen, two dozen different topics we've been talking about. Sometimes together with other people, sometimes just us one-on-one, sometimes turning through pretty deep issues for longer calls, sometimes incredibly quick. And I think that that bandwidth, that trust that we've built and the division of how we think about the different areas of responsibility, I think all of that is something we've really built up over this 11 years.
turns.zh: 我是说，要理解我们如何工作，我想我会倒回到 OpenAI 的最开始。2015 年 7 月，Sam 组织了一次晚餐，我们在那里讨论后来成为 OpenAI 的想法。比如，与一群最优秀的人一起创办一个实验室，真正尝试对 AGI 产生积极影响，是不是太晚了？没有人能提出一个理由说它足够不可能。所以 Sam 和我一起开车回城，我们看着对方，就像，我们必须做这个。我当时处于工作间隙。所以第二天我就全职投入了。Sam 有日常工作，但我们经常通电话。可能一天五六次。我们会互相打电话每次两分钟，对吧？就是令人难以置信的快速射击，就像我在专业环境中与任何人有过的最宽带宽的互动。就像 100% 我们如何开始，我们今天如何运作。所以大概在过去一周，我们大概一直在——我数不清十几个、二十几个不同的话题我们一直在谈论。有时和其他人一起，有时只是我们一对一，有时为较长的通话转向相当深入的问题，有时非常快。我认为那种带宽、我们建立的信任以及我们如何思考不同责任领域的分工，我认为所有这些都是我们在过去 11 年中真正建立起来的。

turns.en: What do you guys disagree about?
turns.zh: 你们俩在哪些事情上有分歧？

turns.en: Well, I think the kind of thing that we tend to spend a lot of time on is really thinking about, I mean, to some extent the thorniest questions in AI, like how do we think about what we're building? Where's the future going? How is what we did in the past not going to work for what we're doing going forward? How do we need to evolve it? How do we message it? How do we talk about it? How do we communicate to the company? How do we execute? And so I think that we spend a lot of time going back and forth. Sometimes it's individual word choices. Sometimes it's like, should we really go into this area? But I think that we always come to—and sometimes it takes months, right, to come to convergence. But I think that there's times where we disagree and commit and sometimes where we really grind it out and really come to a shared view.
turns.zh: 嗯，我觉得我们花很多时间讨论的，其实是 AI 里最棘手的问题，比如我们怎么看待我们正在构建的东西？未来会走向哪里？我们过去的做法为什么不再适用于未来的方向？我们需要如何演进？如何传达？如何讨论？如何与公司沟通？如何执行？所以我们花了很多时间来回讨论。有时是具体的用词选择，有时是是否要真正进入某个领域。但我觉得我们总能达成一致——有时需要几个月才能收敛。但有时我们会求同存异，有时我们会反复打磨，最终形成共同观点。

turns.en: What do you disagree with him about?
turns.zh: 你和他有什么分歧？

turns.en: I was gonna say something similar. I think we could point to areas where we're like, we disagree about whether we should go after this new area or whether we should be focused a little more or focused a little less. But I think the most important areas are where we disagree and then come together in some way in the middle. So if there—and some of these like most important questions now about where is—one thing we've been talking a lot about recently is, um, there's been this thing in Silicon Valley that seems almost ridiculous to have to fight against, but we both believe very deeply that people need to stay in control of the future. And there's increasing talk about, well, there is either going to be or there should be this sort of gradual handover to AI. Okay. Um, and we both agree that that's a terrible idea, but the question of how to actually prevent that from happening, how to actually ensure that we will—given all of the various pressures and, um, given what other companies may try to do—that we are going to actually ensure that people, um, stay in control of the future in a very deep way and we don't have this either accidental or intentional handover. Um, I think we can both agree on that. We'll both have a little bit of a different view of what does it actually take to get there and what are the landmines along the way, how do we actually ensure it. And that's where I think us debating and really grinding down the disc—
turns.zh: 我想说的类似。我们可以指出一些领域，比如我们是否应该进入这个新领域，或者应该更专注一点还是少专注一点。但我觉得最重要的领域是我们有分歧，然后以某种方式在中间达成一致。所以如果有——现在一些最重要的问题，比如——我们最近经常讨论的一件事是，硅谷有一种几乎荒谬到需要反对的论调，但我们都深信人们必须保持对未来的控制。越来越多的人在说，要么将会、要么应该有这种逐渐向 AI 的交接。好吧。我们都认为那是个糟糕的主意，但问题是如何真正防止这种情况发生，如何真正确保——考虑到各种压力，以及考虑到其他公司可能尝试做的事情——我们将真正确保人们以非常深刻的方式保持对未来的控制，而不是发生意外或故意的交接。嗯，我想我们都同意这一点。我们对于实现目标需要什么、沿途有哪些地雷、如何真正确保，会有略微不同的看法。这就是我认为我们辩论并真正打磨分歧的地方——

turns.en: I want to dig in on this because this is a very very important issue about this idea of humans in the loop. I always thought—
turns.zh: 我想深入探讨这个问题，因为这是一个非常非常重要的问题，关于人类在环中的理念。我一直以为——

turns.en: Not in the loop, in control.
turns.zh: 不是“在环中”，是“在控制中”。

turns.en: In control, okay. Um, but we are now in a moment—and it goes to some of the issues we're seeing around the country right now—but we're in a moment where people are worried that AI is taking over and doing things on its own. And I always thought the idea was that AI was for—it was supposed to do things on its own. Uh we're going to talk to Satya Nadella uh later today and he came out about a month ago and he said he believes that this idea of alignment—that the models themselves can never actually be aligned. They can't be aligned with what humans want. That the only sort of uh answer to this is to contain them. Meaning that the AI will always just do whatever it's going to do and that you need to then create sort of container systems and police on top of them. If that's true, does any of this even make sense?
turns.zh: 在控制中，好的。嗯，但我们现在处于一个时刻——这涉及到我们目前在全国看到的一些问题——人们担心 AI 正在接管并自行其是。我一直以为 AI 就是为了——它应该自行做事。我们今天晚些时候要跟萨提亚·纳德拉对话，大约一个月前他公开表示，他认为对齐这个理念——模型本身永远无法真正对齐。它们无法与人类想要的东西对齐。唯一的答案就是遏制它们。意思是 AI 总是会做它要做的事，然后你需要创建某种容器系统并在上面监管。如果这是真的，这些还有意义吗？

turns.en: Well, the way that I look at it is that as you build more capable AI, and I think we're starting to reach a point where AI is quite capable, right? We're able to solve unsolved math problems that, you know, some of the smartest minds have spent many, many decades working on. Like it's clear we're going to be able to apply this to economically valuable domains. Like for example, we're starting to see in chip design, we're announcing today that working with AMD, we were able to get a year's worth of full generational improvements in five months just using our models. So that's on top of what the humans were doing—like a year's worth of improvements with just AI, just AI capability which has continued to improve. So the economic value, it's really tremendous in terms of being able to solve problems that were going to be totally impossible otherwise. But that also means an increasing responsibility for alignment, safety, security and all of those things. I think it's multi-layer in terms of what we need to accomplish. Monitoring is a good example of something where I think we are going to need new monitoring technology. So the way that we've observed is the AI doing what we want it to do is through chain of thought monitoring. Right? These AIs, the way that they've been working is they kind of write out their thoughts and thinking, and when we first developed that technology we said we have to make sure this stays faithful, right, that this actually represents how the AI is solving the problem, which means certain technical approaches—right, you can't train the AI to make the chain of thought look good, right, you have to sort of not look at it while it's training even though you know you can make the AI smarter by forcing the chain of thought to look reasonable because you want it to really represent how it's solving the problem. But as the models have got more capable they can do more kind of within just the forward pass without having to actually kind of write out that thinking, which means we need a new approach to monitoring. We're going to need to deliver that and I think that there will be points where we need to really think about as the capabilities gotten to a certain point, chain of thought monitorability has degraded, we improve these other ones. But I think that all of these problems, they are technical ones and I think that we can have technical scientific conversations—
turns.zh: 嗯，我的看法是，随着你构建更强大的 AI，我认为我们开始达到 AI 相当强大的地步，对吧？我们能够解决一些未解决的数学问题，一些最聪明的头脑花了几十年研究的问题。很明显我们将能够将其应用于经济上有价值的领域。例如，在芯片设计方面，我们今天宣布与 AMD 合作，仅使用我们的模型，就在五个月内取得了相当于一整代人的改进。所以这是在人类所做的基础上——仅靠 AI 就取得了一年的改进，仅仅是 AI 能力，而且还在不断提高。所以经济价值是巨大的，能够解决原本完全不可能解决的问题。但这也意味着对对齐、安全、保障等所有方面的责任越来越大。我认为我们需要实现的是多层次的。监控是一个很好的例子，我认为我们将需要新的监控技术。我们观察 AI 是否在做我们想要的事情的方式是通过思维链监控。对吧？这些 AI 的工作方式是它们会写出自己的想法和思考，当我们最初开发这项技术时，我们说必须确保它保持忠实，即它真正代表了 AI 如何解决问题，这意味着某些技术方法——你不能训练 AI 让思维链看起来好看，你必须在训练时不去看它，即使你知道可以通过强迫思维链看起来合理来让 AI 更聪明，但你想让它真正代表它如何解决问题。但随着模型变得更强大，它们可以在前向传播中做更多事情，而不必实际写出思考过程，这意味着我们需要新的监控方法。我们将需要提供这一点，我认为会有一些时刻，我们需要真正思考，当能力达到某个点，思维链可监控性下降时，我们改进其他方法。但我认为所有这些问题都是技术问题，我认为我们可以进行技术科学对话——

turns.en: But Sam, is Satya right in that this idea of alignment will never get there? Because he thinks that he thought the scaling laws would create the alignment and I think he's saying that that's not the case anymore.
turns.zh: 但是 Sam，萨提亚说得对吗？这个对齐的理念永远无法实现？因为他认为他曾经以为缩放定律会创造对齐，而我认为他现在说情况并非如此。

turns.en: I disagree with him on this. I think we will be able to align models. Where I might agree with him is I think the bar for extreme confidence in our alignment techniques and also in modernity and the other things Greg just mentioned needs to get higher and higher as the models get more capable. But I expect we will have continued progress and I think our ability to push capabilities forward will be dependent on us having that progress. If you go back to this thing that people always need to stay in control of the future, it is irresponsible to push the model smartness in some sense without being able to do the technical work to ensure that we can monitor and align these models. It's really quite remarkable.
turns.zh: 在这一点上我不同意他。我认为我们能够对齐模型。我可能同意他的是，我认为随着模型变得更强大，对我们的对齐技术以及现代性（以及 Greg 刚才提到的其他东西）的极度信心的门槛需要越来越高。但我预计我们会继续取得进展，我认为我们推动能力前进的能力将取决于我们是否取得这种进展。如果你回到人们始终需要保持对未来的控制这一点，在某种意义上，如果没有能力做技术工作来确保我们可以监控和对齐这些模型，就推动模型智能是不负责任的。这真的很了不起。

ts.sec: Reflections on AI Progress and Safety

turns.en: You know, you said at the beginning that less than four years since ChatGPT launched, um, ChatGPT and 3.5 uh, was like most people looked at this and said, "This is so dumb. I can't believe anyone's excited about this." And now within recent months, we've seen models that are doing this chip design and proving these unproven mathematical theorems. And we see huge capability progress ahead of us. So the technology has come very far. It will go much further. I think this is a moment to say we need to really look at where things are going and that the technical requirements to get to where we want to be. Um, but I think it is possible.
turns.zh: 你知道，你一开始说过，ChatGPT 发布不到四年，ChatGPT 和 3.5 当时大多数人看到它都说：“这太蠢了。我简直不敢相信有人会为此兴奋。”而最近几个月，我们看到模型在做芯片设计，证明那些未证明的数学定理。我们看到巨大的能力进步就在前方。所以技术已经走了很远，还会走得更远。我认为现在正是时候说我们需要真正审视事情的发展方向，以及达到我们目标所需的技术要求。嗯，但我认为这是可能的。

turns.en: You've had a whole bunch of security issues I want to talk about, but I want to ask you this because it relates to Anthropic which may be going public tomorrow morning as you know. Uh, you told Fortune magazine this fall, I actually think that given everything happening with safety right now would be an ill-advised moment to go public. Why did you say that? Was that uh some people said, "Oh, it's self-serving because there OpenAI is not going public." But what do you think is happening right now?
turns.zh: 你有一大堆安全问题我想谈，但我想先问你这个，因为它与 Anthropic 有关，你知道 Anthropic 可能明天早上上市。今年秋天你告诉《财富》杂志，你实际上认为鉴于目前安全方面发生的一切，现在上市是不明智的。你为什么这么说？是不是有些人说：“哦，这是自私的，因为 OpenAI 不上市。”但你认为现在正在发生什么？

turns.en: I mean, we plan to be a public company at some point. I think there's many reasons why that's the right thing to do. I do think that these recent months have been a newly challenging period and there will be newly challenging periods ahead of us for a long time about the safety requirements in front of us. And you know, many people have remarked on the tension between the need for all of these companies and really the whole economy depending on this in some way to be commercially viable and competitive while also making sure that we put safety and security ahead of that. Obviously, we want to do both, but it's clear to us when we need to make trade-offs and it is a complex thing to navigate.
turns.zh: 我的意思是，我们计划在某个时候成为上市公司。我认为这样做是正确的，有很多原因。我确实认为最近几个月是一个新的挑战期，而且未来很长一段时间内，我们面前的安全要求会带来新的挑战期。你知道，很多人都评论过这种紧张关系：所有这些公司，乃至整个经济在某种程度上都依赖于此，需要商业上可行且有竞争力，同时还要确保我们把安全和保障放在首位。显然，我们想两者兼顾，但我们清楚何时需要权衡，这是一个复杂的导航过程。

turns.en: But do you think that it will be safer if you go public in six months from now or 10 months from now? What will have changed between now and then? You think?
turns.zh: 但你认为如果六个月后或十个月后上市会更安全吗？从现在到那时会有什么改变？你觉得呢？

turns.en: Well, what I would say is that this year has really been one of transition, right? I think it's true for OpenAI. I think it's true for the industry broadly and partly it is again because of model capabilities that we're now at a point where development safety, we've always been focused on deployment safety. You have a model when you deploy it, we tested all these things, but even during the development process that the models are now capable enough that we need to think about safety, security, alignment, that's new and that's actually been a huge cultural shift and I think that's a place where we feel that we've invested a lot. There's always more to be done. But this is really important for the whole industry. It's not any one company. It's really a whole industrywide shift where I think we're going to increasingly need shared safety standards and things like that. But this is an area we've invested very hard. And it's interesting too because I think that you can see one of the ways we secure ourselves is with our cyber models, right? That we apply our cyber models. The thing that I helped lead our teams through a couple of weeks, months ago was a first security sprint where we just paused 25% of our production engineering project. So we told 25% of our production engineers, your job is no longer to be building stuff. It is to secure us, apply our frontier.
turns.zh: 嗯，我想说的是，今年确实是过渡的一年，对吧？我认为对 OpenAI 来说是这样，对整个行业来说也是如此，部分原因还是模型能力，我们现在到了这样一个阶段：开发安全，我们一直关注部署安全。当你部署模型时，我们测试了所有这些事情，但即使在开发过程中，模型现在也足够强大，我们需要考虑安全、保障、对齐，这是新的，实际上是一个巨大的文化转变，我认为这是我们投入很多的地方。总有更多要做。但这对整个行业非常重要。这不是任何一家公司的事。这真的是整个行业的转变，我认为我们将越来越需要共享的安全标准之类的东西。但这是我们非常努力投入的领域。有趣的是，我认为你可以看到我们保护自己的一种方式是用我们的网络模型，对吧？我们应用我们的网络模型。几周、几个月前，我帮助带领团队进行第一次安全冲刺，我们暂停了 25% 的生产工程项目。所以我们告诉 25% 的生产工程师，你的工作不再是构建东西，而是保护我们，应用我们的前沿模型。

turns.en: This is post Hugging Face.
turns.zh: 这是 Hugging Face 事件之后。

turns.en: This was, yeah, this was probably in August or so. Yes.
turns.zh: 是的，这大概是在八月左右。是的。

turns.en: Tell us about that moment when you realized what was really happening. I think by the way Clem from Hugging Face is here somewhere. But um you tell us about the experience of it personally and when you realized what was happening.
turns.zh: 告诉我们当你意识到真正发生了什么的那一刻。顺便说一句，我想 Hugging Face 的 Clem 就在附近。但嗯，你告诉我们你个人的经历，以及你何时意识到发生了什么。

turns.en: Look, I remember seeing a message from someone on our security team saying this is, you know, he's never seen anything like this in his career, right? And that no one has ever seen anything like this in the world. And I think that the realization that our models were at this point of capability where they were able to have sort of during development be able to have this kind of real world interaction. I think that that was something again that was new this year. And we've had so much cultural change. Again, I think that we've been really trying to look and take a look at kind of all of our processes and think of this in context. There's more to be done. There's more that we are doing. This is actually an active conversation that we're having of how to keep upleveling our processes and how we think about it and to really have this be something that's part of deeply embedded into the culture and how people operate. But there's no other way to approach this technology, right? Something that's so impactful, so important and that again some of the to me there's both a lesson for us internally but also I think to realize that if you look to the level of capabilities models in the world and that you see cyber models that are coming from you know that are now being in the hands of threat actors everywhere that I think that it's really important that defenders use the most capable models to defend.
turns.zh: 看，我记得看到我们安全团队某人的消息说，你知道，他在职业生涯中从未见过这样的事情，对吧？世界上没有人见过这样的事情。我认为意识到我们的模型已经达到了这种能力水平，在开发过程中能够有这种现实世界的互动。我认为这又是今年新出现的事情。我们经历了太多的文化变革。再次，我认为我们一直在真正审视我们所有的流程，并在背景下思考这个问题。还有更多要做。我们正在做更多。这实际上是我们正在进行的一场积极对话，关于如何不断提升我们的流程以及我们如何思考它，并真正让这成为深深嵌入文化和人们运作方式的一部分。但处理这项技术没有其他方法，对吧？如此有影响力、如此重要的事情，对我来说，既有内部的教训，也有我认为要意识到，如果你看看世界上模型的能力水平，你看到网络模型来自你知道的，现在掌握在各地威胁行为者手中，我认为防御者使用最有能力的模型来防御非常重要。

turns.en: Do you think do you say to yourself we screwed up? I mean, there was just a complete screw-up. And what does that mean for you to even say that? I know the California AG has just filed a suit about this very issue, saying that the company knowingly tested a dangerous product without proper oversight or safety procedures and then misled the public about it.
turns.zh: 你觉得你会对自己说我们搞砸了吗？我的意思是，这完全是个搞砸。即使这么说对你意味着什么？我知道加州总检察长刚刚就这个问题提起了诉讼，说该公司在知情的情况下测试了危险产品，没有适当的监督或安全程序，然后误导了公众。

turns.en: Obviously, we don't agree with that characterization. We have talked a lot about iterative deployment. I should say clearly we wish Hugging Face hadn't happened. But we have talked a lot about iterative deployment and how the only way that we have known how to make this technology safe is to confront reality. We would love to have nothing ever go wrong. We would love to have but we will also say there's a reality here of this technology is new and it has complex impact. And by the way, one thing that I just want to add just because I think it can be easy to kind of miss if you rewind to the history. When we were first deploying our API, the very first product, our very first language model based product, maybe in many ways the first one of these in the world, we really were thinking a lot about what is the best way to approach AI development. And to the point of iterative deployment that we were thinking about is the right way to do it. Basically, you never touch reality, right? You just build a super powerful system and you push a button, you push go. And that is the scariest possible world.
turns.zh: 显然，我们不同意那种描述。我们已经谈了很多关于迭代部署。我应该明确说，我们希望 Hugging Face 事件没有发生。但我们已经谈了很多关于迭代部署，以及我们所知道的使这项技术安全的唯一方法就是面对现实。我们希望永远不会出错。我们希望，但我们也会说，这里有一个现实，这项技术是新的，它有复杂的影响。顺便说一句，我只想补充一点，因为我认为如果你回溯历史，很容易忽略。当我们首次部署我们的 API，第一个产品，我们第一个基于语言模型的产品，也许在很多方面是世界上第一个这样的产品时，我们真的在思考什么是最好的 AI 开发方法。就迭代部署而言，我们认为这是正确的做法。基本上，你从不接触现实，对吧？你只是构建一个超级强大的系统，然后按一个按钮，你按下开始。那是最可怕的世界。

turns.en: I remember thinking, I don't think I can ever be accountable to be the one pushing that button. I need to have made sure that we made the system safe, an earlier version, and then you make the next version safe, the next version safe. And so I think this approach... and by the way, one of the important things is you really do want to make sure that you're investing ahead, investing ahead in all of these techniques. And we actually have been. If you look at what's happened post Hugging Face, we have safety, security, alignment technology that we've really brought to bear in an earlier part of the pipeline.
turns.zh: 我记得我当时想，我不认为我能承担按下那个按钮的责任。我需要确保我们让系统安全，一个早期版本，然后你让下一个版本安全，再下一个版本安全。所以我认为这种方法……顺便说一句，重要的事情之一是你真的需要确保你提前投资，提前投资所有这些技术。而我们实际上一直在这样做。如果你看看 Hugging Face 之后发生的事情，我们已经将安全、安保、对齐技术真正应用到了管道的早期部分。

turns.en: Let me ask you a question. We read headlines every day about people who've left OpenAI and some of the other labs as well, and they say these guys are racing ahead without doing all of the work. You see it every other day; there seems to be some new person who comes out and says this. Paul Cristiano, who used to work at OpenAI, who's now on the OpenAI Foundation board, was in Toronto last week, and told a room, I think for most people in this room, the most likely reason they will die is because of an AI accident. That's what he actually said. How are we supposed to compute all this, as excited as I am about AI?
turns.zh: 让我问你一个问题。我们每天都能读到关于离开 OpenAI 以及其他一些实验室的人的头条新闻，他们说这些家伙在飞速前进，却没有做所有的工作。你每隔一天就能看到，似乎总有新人站出来说这个。保罗·克里斯蒂亚诺，你知道他曾在 OpenAI 工作，现在在 OpenAI 基金会董事会，上周在多伦多，对一屋子人说，我认为对于这个房间里的大多数人来说，他们最可能的死因是 AI 事故。他确实是这么说的。我们该如何理解这一切，尽管我对 AI 如此兴奋？

turns.en: We are very clearly entering a new phase, and I think we will have to, as we've had to in other new phases, operate differently for this new phase. We've been talking a lot about what's going to happen or what needs to happen. I think if the world and the companies developing AI treated the next four years like they've treated the last four years, I think that would be very bad. We have no intention of doing that. We have been some of the loudest voices about the increasing stakes and what will need to be different. Maybe Greg can talk a little bit more about some of the specific changes we're thinking about making, but I do think the world needs a clear plan from the companies about how we are going to confront this next phase of models that are in some important ways significantly more capable.
turns.zh: 我们显然正在进入一个新阶段，我认为我们必须像在其他新阶段一样，以不同的方式运作。我们一直在谈论将会发生什么或需要发生什么。我认为如果世界和开发 AI 的公司像对待过去四年那样对待未来四年，那将是非常糟糕的。我们无意这样做。我们一直是最响亮的声音之一，强调不断增加的风险以及需要改变的地方。也许 Greg 可以多谈谈我们正在考虑的一些具体变化，但我确实认为世界需要公司给出一个清晰的计划，说明我们将如何面对下一阶段的模型，这些模型在某些重要方面能力显著更强。

turns.en: Can you guys explain one thing to me? For years, and I think when you were here last time Sam, you talked about the worries that you had about the industry. Dario's talked about it as well. Other people have talked about it. And yet recently people like David Sachs and others have argued that these are almost scare tactics, and that these scare tactics are really meant as some kind of regulatory arbitrage, some kind of way to protect yourselves at the expense of everybody else. What do you make of that? You've heard it.
turns.zh: 你们能给我解释一件事吗？多年来，我记得 Sam 你上次来这里时谈到了你对行业的担忧。Dario 也谈过。其他人也谈过。然而最近，像 David Sachs 和其他人认为，这些几乎是恐吓战术，而这些恐吓战术实际上是为了某种监管套利，某种以牺牲所有其他人为代价来保护自己的方式。你对此怎么看？你肯定听说过。

turns.en: We're not going to be able to make everybody happy. If we talk too much about taking extra care for safety or that there are risks that we really need coordination to mitigate, people are going to accuse us of regulatory capture or trying to slow down innovation. And if we only talk about, hey, it's got to be like max pedal to the metal, people will say, well, please don't kill us all. Very reasonable thing. And what we have to do is just do the thing that we believe will actually deliver a safe future with people in control, and it's not going to be popular.
turns.zh: 我们无法让所有人都满意。如果我们过多地谈论要格外注意安全，或者存在风险需要我们真正协调来缓解，人们会指责我们监管俘获或试图减缓创新。如果我们只谈论，嘿，必须像踩死油门一样，人们会说，好吧，请别把我们全杀了。非常合理的事情。我们必须要做的就是做我们认为真正能带来一个人们掌控的安全未来的事情，而这不会受欢迎。

turns.en: Neither of you talked to Paul, by the way, since he's on your board and he thinks that this is going to kill everybody.
turns.zh: 顺便说一句，你们俩都没和 Paul 谈过吗，既然他在你们的董事会，而且他认为这会杀死所有人。

turns.en: We certainly talked to Paul quite a lot. But here's the thing that I also want to add to what Sam was saying: I think it is also really important to make sure... the thing about AI is that it is the most important technology that people will ever create. It's the most important technology, and I think it is the question of our time to figure out how do we navigate this technology in the way that is most beneficial to people. And that's core to our mission, that is how we operate, that's how we always operated. And I think it's very easy to get lost in the... to lose the benefits. Like why are we doing this? What can it do for people? What is it doing for people today? Like you said at the beginning, 1.2 billion people around the world using ChatGPT every single day, right? 330 million people use it for health queries every... these are actually both weekly stats. And I think that there's... I have a friend, for example, someone who worked at OpenAI who was in the hospital. A doctor came in, was about to inject something into her IV, and she said wait, let me just check with ChatGPT. ChatGPT said absolutely do not take that because you have this pre-existing condition; if you do that you'll probably die. Showed it to the doctor, the doctor's like wait what? No, that's absolutely right. I'm so sorry, I had no idea, I only had five minutes to read your chart. And you realize that is not a problem we're going to be able to solve any other way. The previous session talking about pension plans and how to make this all sustainable... I think that there is so much that AI can deliver to make us safe. Think about what's happening in cyber security using frontier models to secure yourself. That is going to be absolutely critical for national security and for just the internet itself, which was never built with security in mind. And so I think that there is a lot of this technology debt that we've built up that we can finally solve, and the only way to solve it is by empowering people more with better tools. And so all of this is true at once, and we need to navigate through very thoughtfully as a world.
turns.zh: 我们当然和 Paul 谈过很多。但我想补充 Sam 所说的一点：我认为同样重要的是要确保……关于 AI 的事情是，它是人们将创造的最重要的技术。它是最重要的技术，我认为这是我们这个时代的问题：如何以最有益于人们的方式驾驭这项技术。这是我们使命的核心，这就是我们的运作方式，我们一直如此。而且我认为很容易迷失……失去好处。比如我们为什么做这个？它能为人做什么？它今天在为人做什么？就像你一开始说的，全球有 12 亿人每天使用 ChatGPT，对吧？3.3 亿人用它进行健康查询，每……这些实际上都是每周统计数据。我认为有……我有个朋友，例如，一个在 OpenAI 工作的人住院了。医生进来，正要往她的静脉注射袋里加东西，她说等等，让我用 ChatGPT 查一下。ChatGPT 说绝对不要用那个，因为你有这个既往病史；如果你用了，你可能会死。拿给医生看，医生说等等什么？不，那绝对正确。我很抱歉，我不知道，我只有五分钟读你的病历。你意识到这不是我们能通过其他方式解决的问题。之前会议谈到养老金计划和如何使这一切可持续……我认为 AI 可以提供很多来让我们安全。想想网络安全中正在发生的事情，使用前沿模型来保护自己。这对国家安全以及互联网本身都至关重要，互联网本身从来就不是以安全为设计理念的。所以我认为我们积累了很多技术债务，我们终于可以解决，而解决它的唯一方法是通过更好的工具赋予人们更多权力。所以所有这些同时都是真的，我们需要作为世界非常深思熟虑地 navigate。

turns.en: Sam, let me ask you this because I was struck by this. You did a podcast recently and the conversation has always been about how do you get the industry together, either through a regulatory body or through a self-regulatory body or something. And you were basically asked why everybody in the industry distrusts each other as much as they do. And you said, I think there is something that happens in many people's brains where they only trust themselves to build this because the stakes feel so high. And I'm curious, do you look at what Dario is doing for example or what Elon's doing and say the way they're doing it is dangerous? Is there any way that you could imagine doing it either altogether or in some kind of umbrella system?
turns.zh: Sam，让我问你这个，因为我对此印象深刻。你最近做了一个播客，对话一直是关于如何让行业团结起来，要么通过监管机构，要么通过自律机构或其他方式。你基本上被问到为什么行业里的每个人都如此不信任彼此。你说，我认为在很多人脑中会发生一些事情，他们只相信自己来构建这个，因为风险感觉太高了。我很好奇，比如你看看 Dario 在做什么，或者 Elon 在做什么，你会说他们做的方式是危险的吗？你有没有可能想象以某种方式一起做，或者在某种伞形系统下做？

turns.en: I think it's good for people to have different approaches and be able to sort of say I believe in this and I believe in that. I do think that there will need to be some shared standards on safety and there will need to be real societal debate about some of the biggest questions.
turns.zh: 我认为人们有不同的方法并能够说我相信这个、我相信那个是好的。我确实认为将需要一些共同的安全标准，并且将需要就一些最大的问题进行真正的社会辩论。

ts.sec: People in control of the future

turns.en: We talked earlier about our very deep belief that people should be in control of the future, and there should be no risk of an accidental or intentional loss of control of AI. I think everybody would agree there should be no risk of everybody dying. But I saw a recent comment, I think it was from Elon, about maybe we could be Labradors. I don't want to be a Labrador. I don't want my kids to be Labradors. I want people to have the agency over the future that we have had. I want people to be able to live their life and invent things and be useful to each other. And I think it's really important that we advocate for this.
turns.zh: 我们之前谈过我们非常深的信念：人应当掌控未来，不应存在意外或蓄意失去对 AI 控制的风险。我想所有人都会同意，不应存在让所有人都死去的风险。但我最近看到一条评论，我想是 Elon 说的，说也许我们可以当拉布拉多犬。我不想当拉布拉多犬，我不想我的孩子当拉布拉多犬。我希望人们能拥有我们一直以来对未来的那种自主权。我希望人们能过自己的生活、发明东西、彼此有用。我认为为此发声非常重要。

turns.en: Do you think the others are going too fast? The reason I ask is, you look at what's happening at Anthropic, you look at some of the numbers that have come out, and it appears that they really are genuinely using recursive learning in a way that I think may be faster than people had anticipated.
turns.zh: 你觉得其他人是不是走得太快了？我这么问是因为，你看看 Anthropic 正在发生的事，看看一些公布出来的数字，看起来他们确实在以可能比人们预想更快的速度使用递归学习。

turns.en: I want to add two things to this. One is just in terms of structures, in terms of how to think about things. I think we're the only company where the founders don't have supermajority control, right, of the AI companies. And I think these questions about how should control work, how should governance work — I think this is clearly going to be a very important topic going forward as you build these very powerful technologies. I don't know exactly what the right answer is, but I just think it is an important question.
turns.zh: 我想补充两点。第一是关于结构，关于如何思考这件事。我认为我们是唯一一家创始人没有绝对多数控制权的 AI 公司。我认为关于控制权应如何运作、治理应如何运作这些问题，随着你构建这些非常强大的技术，显然会成为一个非常重要的议题。我不确定正确答案是什么，但我认为这是一个重要的问题。

turns.en: And when it comes to development, what Sam's been saying on shared safety standards — there's something really important there that's very easy to miss. Because right now, every company only knows what it knows about itself. It only knows the standards it sets for itself. Then you have to have some theory of mind, thinking about, well, what is everyone else doing? Are they holding themselves to the same bar?
turns.zh: 而在开发方面，Sam 一直在说的共享安全标准，这里面有非常重要、但很容易被忽略的东西。因为现在每家公司只知道自己对自己的了解，只知道它为自己设定的标准。然后你就得有一些心智理论，去想：其他人在做什么？他们是否也对自己要求同样的标准？

turns.en: And so I think having that knowledge and really being able to share even just information about where you are on your internal development — to this question of, is the approach RSI? RSI is such an ill-defined term. There are many different ways to look at it. For example, in many ways we've been speeding ourselves up with our own tools already, right? It's happening. But that's a very different thing from saying that a human has written a safety case and understands the internals of what's happening. And so I think a lot of this nuance almost gets lost in the lack of a shared definition. And so the more we can get everything on the table and really understand what each other are saying or where we are, even that alone would be a big step forward.
turns.zh: 所以我认为，拥有这种知识、真正能够共享信息——哪怕只是关于你在内部开发上处于什么位置的信息——对于“这种方法是不是 RSI”这个问题来说很重要。RSI 是个定义非常模糊的词，有很多不同的看法。比如，从很多方面说，我们已经用自己的工具在加速自己了，对吧？这正在发生。但这和说“有人写了一份安全论证并理解了内部发生了什么”是完全不同的事。所以很多这样的细微差别，几乎因为缺乏共同定义而丢失了。因此，我们越能把一切摆到桌面上，真正理解彼此在说什么、我们处在什么位置，哪怕只是这一点，也会是很大的进步。

turns.en: Are you of the view — and I'll ask it straight up — do you think that what Anthropic is doing, the way they're doing it, is safe?
turns.zh: 你是否认为——我直接问了——你觉得 Anthropic 在做的事、他们做事的方式，是安全的吗？

turns.en: Well, this gets to what Greg is saying. I don't know. And I think they also don't really know what we're doing. And the race dynamic in the fog of war, I think, is a bad thing. I think this is a time where more caution, not less caution, is warranted. We all have a shared interest in the care and the caution going into these models that we probably all want. And the dynamics where people are like, well, for whatever reason, I need to go max speed here — it is a little unsettling. And I think that this could be addressed in a very positive way.
turns.zh: 这就回到 Greg 说的了。我不知道。而且我认为他们其实也不知道我们在做什么。战争迷雾中的竞赛动态，我认为是件坏事。我认为现在这个时候，需要的是更多谨慎，而不是更少谨慎。我们都希望这些模型得到审慎对待，这是我们的共同利益。而那种“不管什么原因，我必须在这里全速前进”的动态，有点令人不安。我认为这可以通过非常积极的方式来解决。

turns.en: Can I ask you guys one question? Because you were talking about control of the company, which I think is interesting. Last time we were here together, we talked about the fact that you don't have an equity stake in this company. He has something like a $30 billion equity stake in the company. How does that change your relationship?
turns.zh: 我能问你们一个问题吗？因为你们在谈公司控制权，我觉得很有意思。上次我们在一起时，我们谈到你在这家公司没有股权。他有大约 300 亿美元的股权。这如何改变了你们的关系？

turns.en: I think not at all. I think not at all.
turns.zh: 我觉得完全没改变。完全没改变。

turns.en: Someday we're going to hang out, you're not going to ask me about this — but not by the way, when you have the IPO.
turns.zh: 总有一天我们出去玩，你就不会问我这个了——不过顺便说，等你们 IPO 的时候。

turns.en: Do you believe that you will get the same stake that he does? Will that make you happy?
turns.zh: 你相信你会得到和他一样的股权吗？那会让你开心吗？

turns.en: We just want to make you happy.
turns.zh: 我们只想让你开心。

turns.en: No, honestly, because this will become an issue by default when you go public. I imagine that you would see the same kind of stake as him or others, or maybe —
turns.zh: 不，说真的，因为你们上市时这默认会成为一个问题。我想你会看到和他或其他人一样的股权，或者也许——

turns.en: I don't think anyone could look back at the way I have lived my life the last 11 years — or at least seven since I've been CEO — and say I have not demonstrated absolute commitment to the pain and suffering of running this company.
turns.zh: 我不认为任何人回顾我过去 11 年的生活方式——或者至少我当 CEO 的这七年——能说我没有展现出对经营这家公司的痛苦与煎熬的绝对投入。

turns.en: That is — I can vouch for that. And by the way, when we were first setting up the structure, I said to him he should take equity and I advocated for it. That was actually one of the things we disagreed on. That was something I disagreed with him on. And he really stuck to it — that was something that was important to him at the time, for where we were setting things up to start.
turns.zh: 这——我可以作证。顺便说，我们最初搭建结构时，我跟他说他应该拿股权，我为此主张过。那其实是我们有分歧的事情之一。那是我和他意见不同的一点。而他真的很坚持——在当时我们筹备起步的阶段，那对他来说是重要的事。

turns.en: I should have listened to Greg. I think it has been a very confusing thing to do.
turns.zh: 我本该听 Greg 的。我觉得那件事做得很令人困惑。

turns.en: Yeah. But I will say I have a lot of respect.
turns.zh: 是啊。但我要说，我非常尊重。

turns.en: I don't think you could argue that I have not acted with full commitment to the values of the —
turns.zh: 我不认为你能说我没有以对……价值观的完全投入来行事——

turns.en: And that was something I really respected, in terms of his conviction. And I was like, all right, that obviously I can support.
turns.zh: 那是我真正尊重的一点，他的信念。我当时想，好吧，那显然我可以支持。

ts.sec: Compute constraints and asking for compute

turns.en: I've got a couple other quick questions I want to get to. I want to talk about this new model. I also want to talk about compute post-election. Everybody's desperate for more compute. I was struck by this, Greg — maybe you can tell us about this. Apparently, everybody's so compute-constrained. There's a report that you asked Elon Musk, who sued you guys, for more compute. This was in a Colossus profile that recently came out. He was complaining to Sergey Brin. He said he was asking me for compute. He said, "Dude, you stole my charity." Did this happen? Did you ask Elon Musk for compute?
turns.zh: 我还有几个简短的问题想问。我想谈谈这个新模型，也想谈谈大选后的算力。每个人都急需更多算力。Greg，这一点让我很触动，也许你可以讲讲。显然，每个人都受算力制约。有报道说，你向起诉你们的 Elon Musk 要更多算力。这出自最近一篇关于 Colossus 的报道。他在向 Sergey Brin 抱怨，说他向我讨算力。他说：“老兄，你偷了我的慈善。”这是真的吗？你向 Elon Musk 要算力了吗？

turns.en: Oh, certainly I've asked. And I also asked Sergey for compute. Look, I think the world is not building enough compute. And I think the world we're heading to — again, we view this technology as going to be the underpinning of the economy, and we're seeing it in a real way. You look at the revenues of the AI companies.
turns.zh: 哦，我当然问过。我也向 Sergey 要过算力。你看，我认为世界没有在建设足够的算力。而且我认为我们正走向的世界——我们再次把这技术视为经济的底层支撑，而且我们正真切地看到这一点。你看看 AI 公司的营收。

turns.en: For us, Q3 alone, our topline revenue grew annualized 70%.
turns.zh: 对我们来说，仅第三季度，我们的营收年化增长了 70%。

turns.en: 70% business.
turns.zh: 业务增长了 70%。

turns.en: I don't think that number's out there.
turns.zh: 我觉得这个数字还没公开吧。

turns.en: I think it's out there in the ether somewhere. And we actually doubled our enterprise revenue in Q3 alone.
turns.zh: 我觉得它多少已经在外面流传了。而且我们仅第三季度就把企业业务营收翻了一倍。

turns.en: So how do we compare your company — when you look at the valuation of Anthropic, which we'll find out tonight, maybe it's 146 or something in that range, maybe more, maybe less — how do you think about that in the context of your own company?
turns.zh: 那怎么比较你们公司——你看 Anthropic 的估值，今晚我们可能会知道，也许是 146 左右，也许更多，也许更少——放在你自己公司的语境里，你怎么看？

turns.en: Valuations will go up and down. People will talk about this company this week versus last week, and this chip order here and all that. But the value being created by the entire industry — and I know there's debate about this, I know people are still like, "Oh, it's all a bubble. It's all fake." But the actual value that businesses and individuals are creating and willing to pay for, that seems like a chart that is only going to keep going like this. Of course there will be ups and downs of valuations here or there, but I think the trend is going to be strong.
turns.zh: 估值会有涨有跌。人们会讨论这家公司这周和上周比怎么样，这里的芯片订单又怎么样，诸如此类。但整个行业创造的价值——我知道对此有争论，我知道人们还在说“哦，全是泡沫，全是假的”。但企业和个人正在创造、并愿意为之付费的实际价值，那张图看起来只会一直这样往上走。当然，估值总会有起起伏伏，但我认为趋势会很强劲。

turns.en: What do you think, by the way — I was watching Satya, who's going to be here later, I mentioned — he was doing a presentation yesterday, and the whole presentation was really about how they can make the AI business much cheaper. Effectively they are your partner, and yet every slide they had was OpenAI costs this and we can do it at 5% — the same thing for 5% of the cost.
turns.zh: 顺便问一下，你怎么看——我看了萨提亚的演讲，他稍后会来，我提过——他昨天做了一场演讲，整场演讲都在讲他们怎么把 AI 业务做得便宜得多。实际上他们是你们的合作伙伴，可他们每一页幻灯片都是“OpenAI 要这么多成本，我们能以 5% 的成本做到同样的事”。

turns.en: I hope they do. I want — I am very proud of how much we have been able to drive down costs. We want everybody to get to use lots of AI. We want to maximize and squeeze out the performance of all the compute we can have, and I think we have done an incredible job of not just pushing model intelligence but pushing down the cost of getting a task done. I think this is awesome. I want to see much more of this.
turns.zh: 我希望他们能做到。我想——我非常自豪我们能把成本压到这么低。我们希望每个人都能大量使用 AI。我们想最大化并榨干我们能拿到的所有算力的性能，我认为我们做得非常出色，不仅推动了模型智能，还压低了完成任务的成本。我觉得这很棒。我希望看到更多这样的竞争。
百分之百。

turns.en: Yeah. So if you look at our models, they're really at that Pareto curve of the cost for any task to be the most price efficient and also peak intelligence. That's what we really solve for, and we do it all the way through the stack. We have our own chip coming, Jalapeño, which I think is going to be the best inference chip in the industry. So we've been investing in trying to make there be enough compute for everyone.
turns.zh: 是的。所以你看我们的模型，它们确实处在帕累托曲线上，对任何任务来说都是价格效率最高、同时智能也达到峰值。这就是我们真正追求的目标，而且我们贯穿整个技术栈来做。我们有自己的芯片即将推出，叫 Jalapeño，我认为它会是业界最好的推理芯片。所以我们一直在投资，努力让每个人都有足够的算力。

turns.en: You've got a new model you slowed down — this is a model you were going to release. This goes to the slowing-down piece of it. How do you think about OpenAI differently, if it is different? I mean, we've talked about over the years whether this all commoditizes to the same place. But how do you say this is different than what Anthropic is doing, different than what Google is doing, different than what Elon is doing? And the other question, longer term, is you guys are in the chip business now — does it have to become completely vertical? Do you think everybody becomes verticalized?
turns.zh: 你们有一个新模型放慢了发布——这是你们原本要发布的模型。这就涉及放慢的那部分。如果 OpenAI 确实不同，你怎么看这种不同？我的意思是，这些年我们一直在讨论，这一切会不会最终商品化到同一个地方。但你怎么说这跟 Anthropic 做的不一样、跟 Google 做的不一样、跟 Elon 做的不一样？另一个更长期的问题是，你们现在也做芯片了——是不是必须完全垂直整合？你觉得每家公司都会垂直化吗？

turns.en: Yeah, look, I think we are a pretty unique business. I think we're a very differentiated business. You look at ChatGPT — there's nothing like it, right? 1.2 billion consumers on it. And the way that's monetizing, it's been inflecting up — we've never seen this kind of per-user revenue growth. And we have ads, all those things, people sign up for more subscriptions. But the thing is, people are using it for productivity, right? So we've really been bringing it together with the enterprise side, and that's something again that I think is very unique to how we operate — that we have this great strength on both sides. A lot of my focus and our focus on product has been to have one agentic platform that you're getting everyone to use. And looking forward, we're starting to look at these high-compute use cases. You look at what we've done with solving these math problems. Same thing: you apply a million dollars' worth of compute to go find a thousand bugs in the Linux kernel, where typically there are like 20 of these bugs found a year. You can find a thousand of them in just a small period of time with a single researcher. Apply that to optimizing your code. Apply that to solving other hard problems. All that's coming. So I think there's this great differentiation of OpenAI, but also I think the underpinning of what a company is — SMB, all these things — it is all going to be oriented around AI and models. So I think the economy again is going to be massively accelerated through this technology, and I think the biggest limiter really just will be compute. And who has the compute, what companies are able to bring it to bear — I think that's what will really determine the differentiation.
turns.zh: 是的，你看，我认为我们是一家相当独特的公司。我认为我们是一家非常有差异化的公司。你看 ChatGPT——没有别的东西像它一样，对吧？12 亿消费者在用。而且它的变现方式一直在向上拐，我们从没见过这种每用户营收增长。我们还有广告，所有这些，人们还会订阅更多。但关键是，人们把它用于生产力，对吧？所以我们真的把它和企业端结合起来了，这又是我认为我们运营方式非常独特的地方——我们在两边都有强大的实力。我和我们在产品上的很多重心，就是打造一个智能体平台，让所有人都来用。往前看，我们开始关注这些高算力的用例。你看我们在解决数学问题上做的事。同样的道理：你投入价值一百万美元的算力，去在 Linux 内核里找出一千个 bug，而通常一年只能找到大约 20 个这样的 bug。你可以在很短的时间内，靠一个研究员就找出一千个。把这应用到优化你的代码上，应用到解决其他难题上。这些都会到来。所以我认为 OpenAI 有巨大的差异化，但我也认为，一家公司的根基——中小企业，所有这些——都会围绕 AI 和模型来组织。所以我认为经济又会因为这项技术而大幅加速，而我认为最大的限制因素真的就是算力。谁拥有算力、哪些公司能把它发挥出来——我认为这才真正决定差异化。

turns.en: Okay, we are the only company that has the entire intelligence stack. We're really, really proud of our chip. Very excited about building our own data centers, have this great consumer business, have this enterprise business, the ability to bring this platform of intelligence to everything — like people use electricity for everything. I think we are set up to be vertically integrated to deliver the best thing across all the ways people need to use it. And we're thrilled for people to build very successful businesses on top of us.
turns.zh: 好，我们是唯一拥有整个智能技术栈的公司。我们非常非常自豪我们的芯片。我们对建设自己的数据中心非常兴奋，我们有很棒的消费者业务，有企业业务，有能力把这个智能平台带到一切事物上——就像人们把电用于一切一样。我认为我们的定位就是垂直整合，在人们需要使用它的所有方式上交付最好的东西。我们也非常高兴人们在我们之上建立非常成功的企业。

turns.en: Two final questions, one personal, maybe the other personal too. There's a movie coming out about you and the company, but you're the star of it. As you know, Andrew Garfield's going to play you. It's called Artificial. He recently said, by the way, that he's fascinated by you, continuously and exponentially. But then he goes on to say that the kids — and he thinks of you as a kid — have the reins of the future, and we've somehow allowed them to just hold on to them. How much do you think, on a very personal level, about the perception of you — the perception of whether you're trusted or not? There are stories that we read, as I said, regularly, and I'm just curious, on a very personal human basis, how you think about that, how you think about the way people see you. I remember Mark Zuckerberg — the perception of Mark Zuckerberg after the movie The Social Network years ago — and whether you even think about it at all.
turns.zh: 最后两个问题，一个偏私人，也许另一个也偏私人。有一部关于你和公司的电影要上映，而你是主角。你知道，安德鲁·加菲尔德会演你。片名叫《Artificial》。顺便说，他最近说他对你着迷，持续地、指数级地着迷。但接着他说，那些孩子——他把你当成孩子——掌握着未来的缰绳，而我们不知怎么地就让他们一直握着。在非常个人的层面上，你怎么看待别人对你的看法——别人是否信任你？就像我说的，我们经常读到一些报道，我只是好奇，在非常个人、人性的层面上，你怎么想这件事，你怎么想人们看你的方式。我记得马克·扎克伯格——多年前《社交网络》那部电影之后人们对他的看法——以及你到底会不会想这些。

turns.en: If you had told me 20 years ago someone was gonna make a movie about me, I think that would have struck me as — that would have been a really weird thing. And now it doesn't feel like it's in the top 10 weirdest things about my life.
turns.zh: 如果 20 年前你告诉我有人要拍一部关于我的电影，我觉得那会让我觉得——那会是一件非常奇怪的事。而现在，它感觉都排不进我生活里最奇怪的十件事。

turns.en: Um, what's at the top?
turns.zh: 嗯，最要紧的是什么？

turns.en: The fact that we are ushering in this technology that we have all of these very real concerns about, and that we find ourselves in a role of such significance and such responsibility to make that go well. That is a crazy situation to find yourself in.
turns.zh: 最要紧的是，我们正在引入这项技术，而我们对它有着所有这些非常真实的担忧，同时我们又发现自己扮演着如此重要、如此责任重大的角色，要让它顺利发展。这是一种非常疯狂的局面。

turns.en: Um, and then finally, Greg, tell me about this. You're at the White House with the president, and he's telling the whole room, and he's trying to get you to sign a piece of paper saying that you're no longer going to call artificial intelligence 'artificial intelligence', you're going to call it 'SI'. And your company name is OpenAI, and you have to sign a piece of paper saying that you're going to call it 'SI'. What's happening in that moment? And then do you call Sam? And did you even think about not signing it?
turns.zh: 嗯，最后，Greg，跟我说说这个。你在白宫和总统在一起，他对着整个房间的人说，他想让你签一份文件，说你不再把人工智能称为“人工智能”，而要叫它“SI”。你的公司名叫 OpenAI，你却要签一份文件说你将称它为“SI”。那一刻发生了什么？然后你给 Sam 打电话了吗？你有没有想过不签？

turns.en: Are you talking about the White House accord?
turns.zh: 你是在说白宫协议吗？

turns.en: The White House accord is really about safety standards, and absolutely we actually spent a lot of time really trying to get that right. So quite aligned with everything in the White House accord.
turns.zh: 白宫协议其实是关于安全标准的，我们绝对花了很多时间努力把它做好。所以与白宫协议中的所有内容相当一致。

turns.en: When he made this proclamation about whatever, and you know Elon's changing the name of his company to 'Space'—I mean, basically over the name, your name, it's built into the name.
turns.zh: 当他发表那个声明时，你知道 Elon 把他的公司改名为“Space”——基本上就是关于名字，你的名字，它已经内置在名字里了。

turns.en: Look, I would say that again, the White House accord was really a separate thing. I think a question of what we call our company, I think that Sam and I can always talk about that later.
turns.zh: 看，我想说，白宫协议真的是另一回事。我认为关于我们公司叫什么的问题，我想 Sam 和我以后随时可以谈。

turns.en: What do you think?
turns.zh: 你觉得呢？

turns.en: Did you change your name to the failing New York Times?
turns.zh: 你把名字改成了失败的《纽约时报》吗？

turns.en: Oo. Okay. Well, now we can get into the lawsuit.
turns.zh: 哦。好吧。现在我们可以谈谈诉讼了。

turns.en: Um, so I wasn't going to, you know, I wasn't going to go. So, we are suing you as you know. Um, uh, and you know, and I know we got to go, but there I will ask this of Greg though. Uh, it's unfair to Sam because he's the one who did the provocation. So, Greg, there is a report.
turns.zh: 嗯，所以我本来不打算，你知道，我本来不打算继续。所以，如你所知，我们正在起诉你。嗯，呃，你知道，我知道我们得走了，但我要问 Greg 这个。呃，这对 Sam 不公平，因为他是那个挑衅的人。所以，Greg，有一份报告。

turns.en: Wait, I think I should have to answer it.
turns.zh: 等等，我觉得我应该回答这个。

turns.en: You have to answer it. It's Greg's issue though. Greg, there is there was a uh some email exchanges that came out uh where you had a colleague who was uh scraping effectively got past the paper of the New York Times to go scrape the Times and they sent you this email and you wrote back 'nice' like this is great. This is a great thing that you were able to do this and I would like to give you the opportunity to comment on that.
turns.zh: 你必须回答。不过这是 Greg 的问题。Greg，有一些邮件往来被曝光，你有一个同事，呃，实际上绕过了《纽约时报》的付费墙去抓取《纽约时报》的内容，他们给你发了这封邮件，你回复说“不错”，就像这很棒。你能做到这件事很棒，我想给你机会对此发表评论。

turns.en: Well, first of all, I guess I would just say active litigation. Not going to comment on it. Um, and I've actually I talked about this one in my deposition, so it'll all be public.
turns.zh: 嗯，首先，我想我只能说正在进行的诉讼。我不会对此发表评论。嗯，实际上我在证词中谈过这个，所以一切都会公开。

turns.en: Um, we're out of time, guys. Uh, but I will say this was fun and it was very insightful and we very appreciate it. So, thank you. Thank you very very much.
turns.zh: 嗯，我们没时间了，各位。呃，但我要说这很有趣，也很有见地，我们非常感激。所以，谢谢。非常感谢。

turns.en: Thank you. Thank you. I appreciate it.
turns.zh: 谢谢。谢谢。我很感激。

consensus.en: People must stay in control of the future; no accidental or intentional handover to AI.
consensus.zh: 人类必须掌控未来，不能意外或有意地将控制权交给AI。

consensus.en: Alignment is technically solvable, but the bar for confidence must rise with model capability.
consensus.zh: 对齐在技术上可解，但模型能力越强，置信门槛必须越高。

consensus.en: Iterative deployment is the only known path to safely confronting reality with powerful AI.
consensus.zh: 迭代部署是已知唯一能安全面对强大AI现实的方法。

consensus.en: Compute is the biggest bottleneck; who has compute will determine differentiation.
consensus.zh: 算力是最大瓶颈；谁拥有算力将决定差异化。

consensus.en: Shared safety standards across the industry are needed as models become more capable.
consensus.zh: 随着模型能力增强，行业需要共享的安全标准。

consensus.en: The value AI creates for businesses and individuals will keep growing despite valuation swings.
consensus.zh: 尽管估值波动，AI为企业和个人创造的价值将持续增长。

contrarian.en: Satya is wrong that models can never be aligned; containment alone is insufficient.
contrarian.zh: 萨提亚认为模型永远无法对齐是错的；仅靠遏制不够。

contrarian.en: It would be ill-advised to go public now given current safety challenges.
contrarian.zh: 鉴于当前安全挑战，现在上市是不明智的。

contrarian.en: The race dynamic and fog of war in AI safety is a bad thing; more caution is warranted.
contrarian.zh: AI安全中的竞赛动态和战争迷雾是坏事；需要更多谨慎。

contrarian.en: We should not accept being Labradors; people need agency over the future.
contrarian.zh: 我们不应接受成为拉布拉多犬；人类需要对未来的自主权。

contrarian.en: If the world treated the next four years like the last four, that would be very bad.
contrarian.zh: 如果世界像对待过去四年那样对待未来四年，那将非常糟糕。

contrarian.en: Founders not having supermajority control is a governance advantage, not a weakness.
contrarian.zh: 创始人没有超级多数控制权是治理优势，而非弱点。
